title: Read the slope, skip the experiment
allegory: Attribution patching is estimating what each of thousands of dimmer switches does to a lamp by measuring how touchy each switch is and multiplying by how far you would turn it, instead of turning every switch off and re-measuring the room.
map: turning one switch off and re-measuring the room
true ablation or activation patching: one forward pass per component

chapters.name: Sixteen thousand switches
chapters.note: switch off every latent, one run each?

cap.1: Your SAE has about 16,000 latents. To learn which ones matter, you would switch each off and rerun the model: 16,000 runs. There has to be a shortcut.
cap.2: Ablating latents one at a time costs a forward pass each, which is infeasible at SAE width. You want every latent's effect from a couple of passes instead.
cap.3: Ablation and activation patching scale as one forward pass per component; at SAE widths (16k latents in [1.3.3]) that is prohibitive for a first sweep.

props.label: touchiness × how far you'd turn it

cap.1: Picture a wall of dimmer switches and one lamp. Instead of flicking each switch, measure how touchy each one is, then multiply by how far you would turn it.
cap.2: Attribution patching estimates each component's patching effect as gradient × change in activation. One backward pass gives every gradient at once, so every estimate is nearly free.
cap.3: A first-order Taylor expansion of the metric around the current activations: Δm ≈ ∇ₐm · (a′ − a). A forward and a backward pass (plus one forward per extra prompt) covers all components.

cap.1: The estimate is slope times step: how touchy the switch is, times how far you would move it. For ablation, 'how far' means all the way to zero.
cap.2: For an SAE latent with activation a, ablation moves it to 0, so the estimate is −a × gradient. Get the metric's gradient once, then score every latent with one elementwise product.
cap.3: With the SAE spliced in, ∂m/∂fᵢ = ∇ₓm · W_dec[i], so latent i's ablation estimate is −fᵢ(∇ₓm · W_dec[i]), vectorised over every latent from a single backward pass.

cap.1: For a small turn, the straight-line guess matches reality. For a big one, reality curves away: the lamp can't pass full glare, but the guess keeps climbing.
cap.2: Attribution patching is a tangent line. It holds for small activation changes and near-linear metrics, and drifts when the change is large or the metric saturates.
cap.3: The error is second order in Δa: curvature from softmax saturation, attention re-routing or LayerNorm breaks it. Prefer logit difference to probability, and check against true patching.

chapters.name: Check the shortcut

left.title: attribution patching
lines: every latent from one backward pass
can miss when effects are big

chapters.verdict: Triage with attribution; confirm the top hits with real patching.

cap.1: The shortcut is for sorting, not for final answers. Use it to shortlist the switches that seem to matter, then flick those few for real.
cap.2: In [1.3.3] you compare attribution estimates with true ablation, latent by latent. Where they agree, trust the shortcut; where they peel apart, spend real forward passes.
cap.3: Standard workflow: attribution patching ranks thousands of components, then activation patching or ablation confirms the top-k. Report both, and say where they disagree.

cap.1: Big models have far too many parts to test one by one. Reading slopes gives you a first map of which parts matter, fast.
cap.2: It is the scalable cousin of activation patching and the idea behind attribution graphs, the next node. Remember its failure mode: big changes and saturated metrics.
cap.3: Scalable attribution is what makes understanding and steering feasible at SAE width: it tells you which latents to inspect, ablate or steer, cheaply enough to try them all.

coda.title: The tangent line versus the real curve

curves.label: true metric as the activation changes

readouts.label: estimate ÷ truth
readouts.f: abs(sigmoid(k*(a1 - 1.5)) - sigmoid(k*(a0 - 1.5))) < 1e-6 ? 'no change to estimate' : ((k*sigmoid(k*(a0 - 1.5))*(1 - sigmoid(k*(a0 - 1.5)))*(a1 - a0))/(sigmoid(k*(a1 - 1.5)) - sigmoid(k*(a0 - 1.5)))).toFixed(2)

caption.1: At the start, guess and truth roughly agree. Now set the activation to 3.5 and the curve to 3: the slope goes flat, the guess says 'harmless', truth says huge.
caption.2: The orange line is attribution: the tangent at the current activation. Move the patched value near the current one and they match; move it far or sharpen the curve and they split.
caption.3: On a saturated sigmoid the local gradient vanishes, so a first-order estimate calls a large ablation effect negligible. That false negative is why top and suspicious hits get real patching.

where_else: Saliency maps: gradient × input as a quick guess at which pixels matter
Attribution graphs: the same gradient trick, made well defined by freezing attention patterns and LayerNorm scales
Sensitivity analysis in engineering: estimate each input's effect from derivatives instead of rerunning the simulation

hamming.what: A shortcut that estimates what patching or ablating each component would do, as gradient times activation change, for every component at once.
hamming.when: When there are too many components to patch one by one, like the 16k latents of an SAE in [1.3.3].
hamming.why: It turns thousands of experiments into one backward pass, but it is a straight-line guess, so the important or surprising hits get confirmed with real patching.

object.title: The hillside and its flat map
object.subtitle: The real metric over two activations, and the flat sheet attribution patching swaps in, touching at the clean point.
object.f: (1 - lin)*sigmoid(k*(x + y - 2)) + lin*(sigmoid(k) + k*sigmoid(k)*(1 - sigmoid(k))*(x + y - 3))

cap.1: The real landscape: how the score changes as two activations change. You are standing at the clean point.
cap.2: Metric as a function of two component activations; the clean run sits at (1.5, 1.5).
cap.3: m(a₁, a₂) = σ(k(a₁ + a₂ − 2)): a saturating, probability-like metric over two activations.

cap.1: Attribution swaps in a flat sheet that touches the landscape exactly where you stand. Nearby, it is a good match.
cap.2: The tangent plane at the clean point: attribution patching's model of the metric, exact to first order there.
cap.3: m ≈ m₀ + ∇m · (a − a₀): the plane attribution patching implicitly uses for every component.

cap.1: Walk to the far corner where both are switched off. The flat sheet and the real ground no longer agree.
cap.2: Ablating both is a big move, and the plane's prediction there differs from the true surface.
cap.3: Large Δa exposes the second-order term; the ablation corner is where first-order error is largest.

cap.1: Sharpen the metric: the landscape becomes a cliff, and you are standing on its flat top.
cap.2: A sharper metric saturates: near the clean point the surface is almost level, then drops steeply.
cap.3: Higher k pushes the clean point into saturation, where σ′ ≈ 0 while the ablation effect stays large.

cap.1: Now the flat sheet is nearly level: attribution says nothing here matters, yet switching both off drops you off the cliff.
cap.2: Near-zero gradient means near-zero attribution, even though the true ablation effect is huge: a false negative.
cap.3: Saturation yields vanishing attribution scores for components with large true effects; verify with real patching.

predict.q: Attribution patching estimates a patch's effect as...
predict.why: It is a first-order Taylor estimate: the metric's slope times how far the activation moves.

predict.q: Where is the estimate least trustworthy?

options.t: Big activation changes, or a saturated metric
Small nudges on a near-linear metric

predict.why: A tangent line is only good nearby; curvature such as softmax saturation makes it drift.

predict.q: A latent sits where the metric is saturated, so its gradient is almost 0. Attribution says...

options.t: Ablating it barely matters, possibly wrongly

predict.why: A flat slope gives a near-zero estimate even if real ablation drops the metric off a cliff. Confirm with real patching.

object.where: Any first-order estimate standing in for an expensive experiment: saliency maps, sensitivity analysis.
